title: Impact of Overtime Eligibility Expansion on Work Hours

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy

**Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID)**

This is a classic DID setup. We have:
- A **treated group** (employees newly eligible for overtime pay) and a **control group** (employees unaffected by the policy)
- A **pre-period** and **post-period** around the policy implementation
- The interaction term `treat_x_post` is already constructed, representing the DID estimator

The **key identifying assumption** is the **parallel trends assumption**: absent the overtime eligibility expansion, the treated and control groups would have experienced the same trends in log hours worked. This is plausible if the control group (already exempt or already eligible workers) provides a valid counterfactual for the trajectory of hours worked by newly eligible employees.

We estimate:
$$y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{treated}_i + \beta_2 \cdot \text{post}_t + \beta_3 \cdot \text{treat\_x\_post}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}$$

where $\beta_3$ is the **average treatment effect on the treated (ATT)** — the causal impact of the overtime eligibility expansion on log hours worked.

## 2. R Code

```r
# ============================================================
# DID Analysis: Impact of Overtime Eligibility on Hours Worked
# ============================================================

library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# Load data
df <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s32_data.csv")

# --- Exploratory Summary ---
cat("=== Data Overview ===\n")
cat("Dimensions:", nrow(df), "obs x", ncol(df), "cols\n\n")
cat("Group counts:\n")
print(table(Treated = df$treated, Post = df$post))

cat("\n=== Group Means of y (log hours) ===\n")
group_means <- aggregate(y ~ treated + post, data = df, FUN = mean)
print(group_means)

# Manual DID calculation
y_00 <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 0 & df$post == 0])
y_01 <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 0 & df$post == 1])
y_10 <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 1 & df$post == 0])
y_11 <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 1 & df$post == 1])

did_manual <- (y_11 - y_10) - (y_01 - y_00)
cat("\n=== Manual DID Estimate ===\n")
cat("Control: Pre =", round(y_00, 4), ", Post =", round(y_01, 4), ", Diff =", round(y_01 - y_00, 4), "\n")
cat("Treated: Pre =", round(y_10, 4), ", Post =", round(y_11, 4), ", Diff =", round(y_11 - y_10, 4), "\n")
cat("DID (manual) =", round(did_manual, 4), "\n")

# --- Main DID Regression ---
cat("\n=== Main DID Regression (OLS) ===\n")
model_main <- lm(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, data = df)
summary(model_main)

# Robust standard errors (HC1)
cat("\n=== DID with Heteroskedasticity-Robust SEs (HC1) ===\n")
robust_test <- coeftest(model_main, vcov = vcovHC(model_main, type = "HC1"))
print(robust_test)

# Extract key result
beta_did <- coef(model_main)["treat_x_post"]
se_did <- robust_test["treat_x_post", "Std. Error"]
p_did <- robust_test["treat_x_post", "Pr(>|t|)"]
cat("\n=== KEY RESULT ===\n")
cat("DID Estimate (treat_x_post):", round(beta_did, 4), "\n")
cat("Robust SE:", round(se_did, 4), "\n")
cat("95% CI: [", round(beta_did - 1.96 * se_did, 4), ",", round(beta_did + 1.96 * se_did, 4), "]\n")
cat("p-value:", round(p_did, 4), "\n")

# --- Robustness Check 1: Including unit fixed effects (if repeated obs) ---
cat("\n=== Robustness Check 1: Check for repeated units ===\n")
n_unique <- length(unique(df$unit_id))
cat("Unique unit_ids:", n_unique, "out of", nrow(df), "observations\n")

if (n_unique < nrow(df)) {
  cat("Panel structure detected. Adding unit fixed effects.\n")
  model_fe <- lm(y ~ factor(unit_id) + post + treat_x_post, data = df)
  robust_fe <- coeftest(model_fe, vcov = vcovHC(model_fe, type = "HC1"))
  cat("DID with unit FE:", round(coef(model_fe)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")
  cat("Robust SE:", round(robust_fe["treat_x_post", "Std. Error"], 4), "\n")
} else {
  cat("Cross-sectional (no repeated units). Unit FE not applicable.\n")
}

# --- Robustness Check 2: Randomization/Placebo test ---
cat("\n=== Robustness Check 2: Placebo Test (permuted treatment) ===\n")
set.seed(42)
n_perms <- 1000
placebo_coefs <- numeric(n_perms)
for (i in 1:n_perms) {
  df$fake_treated <- sample(df$treated)
  df$fake_interact <- df$fake_treated * df$post
  placebo_model <- lm(y ~ fake_treated + post + fake_interact, data = df)
  placebo_coefs[i] <- coef(placebo_model)["fake_interact"]
}
p_placebo <- mean(abs(placebo_coefs) >= abs(beta_did))
cat("Proportion of placebo |coefficients| >= |actual DID|:", round(p_placebo, 4), "\n")
cat("This serves as a randomization inference p-value.\n")

# --- Robustness Check 3: Separate pre-period balance check ---
cat("\n=== Robustness Check 3: Pre-period Balance ===\n")
pre_data <- df[df$post == 0, ]
t_test_pre <- t.test(y ~ treated, data = pre_data)
cat("Pre-period mean (Control):", round(t_test_pre$estimate[1], 4), "\n")
cat("Pre-period mean (Treated):", round(t_test_pre$estimate[2], 4), "\n")
cat("Difference:", round(diff(t_test_pre$estimate), 4), "\n")
cat("p-value for pre-period difference:", round(t_test_pre$p.value, 4), "\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings

**Expected sign and magnitude:**

I expect the DID coefficient ($\beta_3$) to be **positive**, indicating that the overtime eligibility expansion **increased** log hours worked for newly eligible employees. The economic intuition is:

- **Substitution effect**: Higher effective wages (overtime premium) for hours beyond the threshold could incentivize workers to supply more hours.
- **Employer behavior**: Employers may restructure work schedules, potentially leading to more formalized (and recorded) hours.

Given the outcome is in **log hours**, I'd expect a moderate effect in the range of **0.05 to 0.30** (roughly 5%–30% increase in hours). However, there's a theoretical ambiguity — employers might also **reduce** hours to avoid paying overtime premiums, which could yield a negative coefficient if the demand-side response dominates.

The effect should be statistically significant if the policy had a meaningful impact. The robustness checks (robust SEs, placebo permutation test, pre-period balance) will help validate that the result is not driven by heteroskedasticity, spurious correlation, or pre-existing group differences.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in log hours worked before and after the policy change between treated and untreated groups.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The expansion of overtime eligibility significantly increased the log hours worked.
